questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: Relationships in the estuary

The fernbird / mātātā (Bowdleria punctata) is a secretive passerine found in wetlands and dense vegetation across New Zealand. It is a cautious species that hunts by walking slowly through raupo stems and sedge margins, searching for spiders, moths, and small invertebrates. Its streaked brown plumage provides excellent camouflage among vegetation.

Fernbirds are primarily active at dawn and dusk (crepuscular). During the breeding season (October to March), pairs produce a series of sharp clucking calls to maintain contact and defend their territory. They nest among dense sedge and rushes, laying 2–4 eggs per clutch, typically once per season.

The introduced Norway rat (Rattus norvegicus) is active mainly at night and is a significant predator of fernbird eggs and chicks.

The introduced common myna (Acridotheres tristis) is active during daylight and competes with fernbirds for invertebrate prey at estuary margins. Mynas are also known to prey on rail eggs opportunistically.

Evaluate reasons for the coexistence and survival of these species in New Zealand estuaries.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the relationships between the fernbird and the Norway rat, AND between the Norway rat and the myna
- an advantage and a disadvantage of being active at dawn and dusk for the fernbird
- how each of the behaviours of these animals support survival, such as nesting among dense sedge for the fernbird, nocturnal foraging for the Norway rat, and diurnal hunting for the myna.
questions.expectedAnswer: Describe predation (Norway rat–fernbird) and interspecific competition (Norway rat–myna for invertebrate prey/eggs); advantage of fernbird being crepuscular (avoids peak activity of both nocturnal and diurnal predators); disadvantage (low light reduces effectiveness of visual foraging).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Describe relationship between Norway rat and fernbird (predation); Norway rat and myna (interspecific competition); advantage of fernbird being crepuscular; disadvantage of fernbird being crepuscular; nocturnal foraging by Norway rat; advantage of nesting in dense sedge; crepuscular/nocturnal behaviour defined; advantage to Norway rat of being nocturnal. Merit: Explain that being active at dawn/dusk allows the fernbird to avoid peak nocturnal predator activity linked to greater chances of survival; fernbird is vulnerable when on the nest at night to mammalian predators which may lead to decreased reproductive success; nocturnal foraging by Norway rat increases its chances of finding food by avoiding diurnal competitors; how nesting in dense sedge provides concealment increasing chances of reproductive success; diurnal myna foraging reduces competition with nocturnal species. Excellence: Discuss predation provides food for Norway rat increasing survival and reproductive success; interspecific competition between Norway rat and myna for similar resources fluctuates seasonally; fernbird being crepuscular provides greater foraging success AND reduced predator encounters increasing survival and reproductive success; nesting in dense sedge when conditions are suitable increases viable offspring survival; nocturnal behaviour of Norway rat synchronises with vulnerable prey activity increasing reproductive success. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=TWO at E, E8=THREE+ at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: Harakeke trees and bellbird

The harakeke / flax (Phormium tenax) produces dark red tubular flowers that are pollinated by birds, including the bellbird / korimako (Anthornis melanura). Plant hormones called auxins play a critical role in the harakeke tree's growth, from root development to stem elongation and flower production.

Bellbird in New Zealand are active during daylight hours (diurnal). They are more active during the warmer parts of the day. Adult bellbird feed on nectar from flowers, while their chicks are fed a diet rich in invertebrates.

Researchers studying bellbird activity in the Waikato region noticed that the birds maintained a regular daily pattern of foraging activity even when kept in constant laboratory conditions with unchanging light and temperature.

Discuss how the control of life processes through biological clocks results in harakeke tree reproductive success.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- whether the harakeke tree is a long-day plant or a short-day plant, including evidence
- the mechanism for the phototropic response of the harakeke stems
- the type of movement response of the bellbird to harakeke nectar
- whether the New Zealand bellbird and the harakeke tree have biological clocks that are entrained to environmental factors.
questions.expectedAnswer: Describe long-day plant (harakeke flowers in NZ late spring/early summer (November–January) when day length exceeds a critical value), phototropism via auxin redistribution, positive chemotaxis of bellbird to nectar, circadian rhythm in bellbird maintained in constant conditions.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Describe a long-day plant; evidence for LDP (long days and short nights induce flowering in late spring/early summer, November–January in NZ); positive chemotaxis or positive trophotaxis; positive phototropism; action of auxin; a named rhythm with definition (e.g. circadian or circannual); the idea of endogenous rhythm maintained in constant conditions; biological clocks; entrainment; a named zeitgeber. Merit: Explain LDP with evidence related to critical day/night length; how auxin redistribution causes phototropism; critical day/night length — uninterrupted darkness duration must be shorter than critical length for flowering; how flowering is caused in long-day and short-day plants; how the bellbird's circadian rhythm persists in constant conditions; how entrainment relates to rhythm; evidence from the laboratory observations for a named rhythm for the bellbird. Excellence: Discuss being able to flower at a specific time of year is important for harakeke success; their biological rhythm is circa-annual and controlled by a biological clock entrained to synchronise with seasonal changes (zeitgeber is photoperiod/day length); flowering needs to coincide with bellbird activity ensuring cross-pollination and increasing genetic diversity; bellbird rely on a biological clock that is endogenously controlled to optimise foraging and pollination behaviours; being active during warmer periods suggests zeitgeber is light intensity but also entrained by temperature. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=TWO at E, E8=THREE+ at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: Cooperative nesting in kea flocks

New Zealand kea (Nestor notabilis) are large alpine parrots known for their flexible social behaviour. They live in loose flocks that collectively defend food-rich territories in native alpine beech forest.

Multiple females may nest in hollows within the same tree or stand, and adults in the flock share responsibilities for mobbing predators, locating food, and calling alarm warnings. The flock typically supports 3–5 nesting pairs per breeding season (October to March).

Dominant individuals secure the best rock crevice nesting sites, while subordinate members (often younger birds or offspring from previous seasons) assist with predator vigilance and food finding. Research has shown that kea preferentially assist relatives more than unrelated flock members.

Kea flocks actively defend territories against neighbouring flocks. Aggressive displays include loud screaming calls, aerial chases, and direct physical confrontation. Access to high-quality forest with abundant fruiting trees is strongly linked to breeding success.

Examine how social behaviour can lead to successful reproduction in kea.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- the terms territory and kin selection, including definitions
- an advantage of communal predator defence and of cooperative vigilance
- why helpers preferentially assist closely related individuals, and why unrelated birds may still remain in the flock
- an advantage and disadvantage of subordinate individuals living in a cooperative group compared to breeding independently.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define territory (a defended area providing resources) and kin selection (individuals assist relatives, increasing the chance shared alleles are passed on). Helpers preferentially assist related individuals because they share alleles.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Define territory; define kin selection; advantage of territory to kea; helpers assist related birds as they share alleles; an advantage of social behaviour e.g. improved predator vigilance; a second advantage e.g. communal mobbing allows adults to forage; unrelated individuals may stay if territory quality is high enough. Merit: Explain defended territory means increased access to resources leading to increased chances of survival and reproduction; kin selection means individuals with common alleles engage in altruistic behaviour to increase chances of alleles being passed on; an example of how social behaviour increases survival e.g. cooperative territory defence; another example e.g. communal vigilance reduces individual energy cost of predator awareness; helpers make genetic contribution by ensuring survival of shared alleles in relatives; unrelated individuals benefit from group protection even if they do not breed. Excellence: Discuss how cooperative behaviour leads to reproductive success — defended territory means chicks raised with less stress and more resources increasing chances of reaching reproductive age; communal defence allows multiple nesting pairs per season increasing total offspring; cooperative vigilance conserves energy increasing survival and reproductive success. Discuss role of kin selection — helpers preferentially assist related birds increasing chick survival and contributing to next generation by ensuring survival of shared alleles; AND discuss why subordinates remain despite costs. Kin selection ensures greater reproductive success due to greater focus on care resulting in greater survival and continuation of shared genes. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=TWO at E, E8=THREE+ at E.
